threads.body:
Consider adding wording to omit the `invoke_workflow` span, in case it happens to be an implementation detail.

Motivating example is using [AgentTool](https://github.com/google/adk-python/blob/ade8577745bda23588bc0ac71f93a9d3343ec80a/src/google/adk/tools/agent_tool.py#L107) in ADK, which uses a `Runner` internally, which means using `AgentTool` produces the following trace.

```
invoke_workflow                            # Entry point for the user
└── invoke_agent root
    ├── chat gpt4-o
    └── execute_tool subagent
        └── invoke_workflow                # ADK implementation detail
            └── invoke_agent subagent
```

I think the nested `invoke_workflow` here only adds noise given:
- With an exception of an exotic [ADK plugin](https://adk.dev/plugins/) setup) only one agent will even be part of this workflow
- Even if another agent is part of the subagent "workflow" here, this span won't create another trace. This is opposed to if we omitted the root `invoke_workflow` span based on a heuristic the setup "looks like a single agent setup".

My rough draft: "The `invoke_workflow` span SHOULD NOT be reported when the workflow invocation is an internal implementation detail of another operation (e.g., an agent or tool that spins up a runner/workflow under the hood to delegate to a sub-agent) rather than a user-facing entry point. In such cases instrumentations SHOULD suppress the nested `invoke_workflow` span so the trace reflects the caller-facing structure instead of framework internals."

threads.body:
This bullet is unqualified, which contradicts "It SHOULD NOT be reported for standalone agent invocations" three paragraphs above. `Runner.run(some_agent, ...)` with no handoffs, no sub-agents, and no agents-as-tools *is* a standalone agent invocation, but this line says every `Runner.run` is a workflow. The ADK bullet got a qualifier; this one didn't, so instrumentation authors get two different answers for the most common case.

```suggestion
      - **OpenAI Agents**: [`Runner.run(starting_agent=...)`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/run/#agents.run.Runner.run) with handoffs, sub-agents, or agents-as-tools.
```

If your intent is instead "every `Runner.run` is a workflow because the SDK itself models it as one" — which is how I read the PR description, and the SDK's own docs do describe it as "Run a workflow starting at the given agent" — then it's the general rule above that needs to soften, not this bullet. Something like: a workflow span MAY be reported when the framework's own entry point is defined as a workflow, even when a particular invocation happens to contain a single agent. Right now the two statements can't both hold.

threads.body:
Two separate things.

**The two omission rules overlap.** "When no meaningful workflow name is available ... this attribute SHOULD NOT be set" and "if there is no low-cardinality workflow name available ... it MUST NOT be captured by default" aren't the same condition — "meaningful" and "low-cardinality" are independent — but they're adjacent and at different strengths, and the example you give (`StateGraph`) is squarely low-cardinality yet discouraged. So a reader whose only available name is `StateGraph` hits both rules and can't tell which governs. Collapsing them would help:

```suggestion
      This attribute MUST have low cardinality. It is NOT RECOMMENDED to use
      instrumentation-time constants or names of types representing the workflow,
      such as "StateGraph". When no meaningful, low-cardinality workflow name is
      available for a given framework, this attribute MUST NOT be captured by default.

      Semantic conventions for individual Generative AI frameworks SHOULD document
      what `gen_ai.workflow.name` means in the context of that framework.
```

Note this deliberately resolves the `SHOULD NOT` / `MUST NOT` mismatch in favor of `MUST NOT`, which is a strengthening — take it only if that's what you meant.

**Trailing whitespace on lines 859 and 863**, which `.editorconfig` disallows (`trim_trailing_whitespace = true`). Line 863 matters beyond tidiness: this is a `note: |` literal block, so that trailing space is copied verbatim into the generated docs — you can see `SHOULD document ` with a trailing space in the diffs of `docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md`, `docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-metrics.md`, and `docs/registry/attributes/gen-ai.md`. (Copilot flagged the same class of thing on the whitespace-only blank lines in `spans.yaml`.)

This comment is inaccurate: it says agent spans are "omitted for brevity", but there are no agents in this graph to omit. `node_a` calls a tool directly and `node_b` formats a string. Worth rewording to describe what the graph actually does.

Separately — and I want to be clear this is a preference, not a defect — I'd push for a more representative graph. Capturability is genuinely fine here: `run_name`, input, and output are all readable at the `graph.ainvoke()` boundary, so this does demonstrate the attributes are collectable, which is the question the rubric actually asks. But the note this PR adds describes workflows as processes "coordinating multiple agents or GenAI calls", and this graph coordinates neither, so as *the* reference example for LangGraph it's thin: a workflow span whose only child is an `execute_tool` span.

`run_plan_and_execute_reference` already shows the pattern for standing up a mock-backed `ChatOpenAI` and emitting the `chat` child span from the captured request/response, and the mock server returns a normal completion for a plain chat call, so having one node do real inference would be cheap. Your call whether that's worth it.

threads.body:
I read the thread with @RKest that produced this sentence, so I understand the case it's for: ADK's `AgentTool` spins up a `Runner` internally, giving you a nested `invoke_workflow` underneath `execute_tool`. My concern is that the sentence as written doesn't carry that meaning to someone who hasn't read the thread.

It's framed around *who calls the operation* — "external callers" vs "internally by the instrumented framework" — but the property that actually separates the motivating case is that the nested invocation is an implementation detail of an enclosing GenAI operation. An instrumentation can detect that (there's an active GenAI span in context when the inner `Runner` starts). Detecting whether its caller was "external" is much less obvious. The sentence also doesn't say what becomes of the internal invocation: suppressed entirely, or reported as something else?

@RKest's draft in that thread is closer to implementable and I'd lean toward it, or something like it:

> The `invoke_workflow` span SHOULD NOT be reported when the workflow invocation is an internal implementation detail of another operation (e.g., an agent or tool that spins up a runner/workflow under the hood to delegate to a sub-agent) rather than a user-facing entry point.

I'm deliberately not putting a suggestion block here, because I don't want to guess at whether you also intend this to cover genuinely nested user-authored workflows (a LangGraph sub-graph invoked as a node of a parent graph). Those look identical in the trace but arguably should keep their span. Whichever way you decide, it's worth saying explicitly.

-      invocations) and SHOULD NOT be reported by instrumentations that
-      can't distinguish it `invoke_workflow` from `invoke_agent`.
-      eg: Some frameworks like ADK have workflow agents that orchestrate other agents
-      and report `invoke_agent` spans, so `invoke_workflow` SHOULD NOT be reported by such instrumentations.
-      Conversely, frameworks like CrewAI have a distinct concept of crew (similar to workflow)
-      that is separate from individual agents, so they SHOULD report `invoke_workflow` spans.
+      The workflow span SHOULD be reported for operations that trigger the execution
+      of composable processes (e.g., graphs, orchestrators) coordinating multiple
+      agents or GenAI calls. It SHOULD NOT be reported for standalone agent invocations.
+
+      If a workflow operation can be invoked both by external callers and internally
+      by the instrumented framework, only the external invocation SHOULD be reported as a workflow span.
+
+      Framework-specific semantic conventions SHOULD define which operations to report
+      as workflows and MAY specify heuristics to distinguish them from standalone
+      agent invocations and internal operations.
+
+      Examples of workflow invocations in different frameworks include:
+
+      - **ADK**: [`Runner.run(...)`](https://adk.dev/agents/) with multi-agent or graph workflow.
+      - **crewai**: [`Crew.kickoff()`](https://docs.crewai.com/concepts/crews)
+      - **langchain / langgraph**: [`*Graph*.invoke(...)`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs)
